unit.title: Leads and the sales pipeline
unit.description: CRM, lead scoring, MQL, SAL, SQL, BANT, lead routing, pipeline, win rate, sales cycle, marketing and sales alignment

cards.definition: Giving each lead points for who they are (fit: job, company size, sector) and what they do (engagement: visits, downloads, demo request). Above a threshold, the lead goes to sales.
cards.example: Plus 20 for a marketing director, plus 30 for a pricing page visit, minus 50 for a student email.

cards.definition: An agreement between marketing and sales: marketing commits to a number of qualified leads, sales commits to follow each one up within a set time. It ends the blame game.
cards.example: Marketing delivers 200 MQLs a month; sales calls every MQL within 24 hours.

cards.definition: A qualified prospect with an identified need, budget and timing, tracked in the CRM with an amount, a stage and an expected close date.
cards.example: Deal: 24,000 euros per year, stage proposal sent, closing expected in March.

exercises.prompt: Put the classic B2B lead stages in order.
exercises.explain: Each stage is a filter: marketing qualifies with behaviour and fit, sales qualifies with a conversation, then a deal is opened.

exercises.prompt: A lead downloaded three guides and attended a webinar, but sales has not talked to them yet. What is it?
choices: An MQL
An SQL
A customer
An opportunity
exercises.explain: Marketing Qualified: the signals come from marketing engagement. It becomes an SQL once sales confirms a real buying project.

choices: Budget, Authority, Need, Timeline
Brand, Audience, Network, Traffic
Budget, Ads, Newsletter, Targeting
Benefit, Action, Need, Trust
exercises.explain: BANT is a classic qualification grid: can they pay, can they decide, do they need it, and when.

exercises.prompt: Which signal should add the most points in lead scoring for a B2B software?
choices: A request for a demo from a target company
A like on a post on LinkedIn
Opening one newsletter
Reading a single blog article
exercises.explain: A demo request shows buying intent; light engagement shows interest at most. Scoring weighs intent and fit.

exercises.prompt: Marketing says sales ignores its leads; sales says the leads are bad. What fixes it first?
choices: A shared lead definition and a marketing and sales SLA
More leads, whatever their quality
Removing the CRM to talk face to face
Paying sales only on the number of calls
exercises.explain: Agree on what a qualified lead is and on follow-up times, then measure both sides against it.

exercises.prompt: You had 50 deals this quarter: 10 won, 30 lost, 10 still open. What is the win rate on closed deals?
choices: 25 percent
20 percent
10 percent
50 percent
exercises.explain: Win rate on closed deals = 10 won divided by 40 closed. Including open deals would understate it.

exercises.prompt: A lead from a company of 5,000 people arrives. What should lead routing do?
choices: Send it at once to the enterprise sales team
Wait one week before anyone looks at it
Put it in the same queue as every student
Delete it if no phone number is filled in
exercises.explain: Routing assigns leads by rules (size, region, product) and speed matters: contact rates drop fast after the first hours.

exercises.prompt: The sales cycle is the time from the first contact with a prospect to the signed deal.
exercises.explain: True. Long B2B cycles (6 to 12 months) mean marketing must nurture leads for a long time and judge results with patience.

exercises.prompt: Why should marketing look at revenue from the pipeline, not only at the number of leads?
choices: Cheap leads that never buy cost more than they bring
Leads are always worth the same amount
Sales prefers to receive fewer leads
Revenue cannot be measured in a CRM
exercises.explain: A campaign with 500 leads and no deals loses to one with 50 leads and 5 deals. Track pipeline and revenue by source.

exercises.title: Fixing a leaking pipeline
exercises.scenario: A SaaS for restaurants generates 800 leads a month. Only 2 percent become customers. Sales calls leads after 4 days on average.

choices: Lead quality by source and the speed of follow-up
The colour of the call to action buttons
The number of posts on Instagram per week
The price of the cheapest plan
steps.feedback: Two suspects: bad leads (fit) and late calls. Both are in the CRM data, by source and by delay.

steps.prompt: Leads called within 1 hour convert 4 times better. What do you set up?
choices: Instant routing plus a 1 hour follow-up rule for hot leads
A weekly meeting to share the lead list
A rule to call every lead on Fridays
Extra forms fields to slow down sign-ups
steps.feedback: Speed to lead: route hot leads instantly and agree on a short SLA. Warm leads can go to nurturing emails.

steps.prompt: Leads from a cheap giveaway campaign never buy. What do you do?
choices: Cut it or score those leads low, and fund the sources that sell
Keep it: it brings the most leads of all
Send all those leads straight to sales
Ask sales to call each of them twice
steps.feedback: Judge sources on deals and revenue, not volume. Volume without fit wastes sales time.

exercises.explain: Measure by source, respond fast, and score leads on fit plus intent.
